description: The Bhakti and Sufi movements played a crucial role in socio-religious reform during Medieval Indian History. They emphasized personal love and devotion to God while strongly opposing rigid rituals, dogmas, and the caste system.

sections.title: Origin and Concepts of Bhakti Movement
sections.description: The fundamental ideologies and core divisions of the Bhakti movement, which originated in South India.

key_concepts.explanation: Worship of God with attributes or form. Followers believed in incarnations (Avatars) of God. Examples: Tulsidas, Mirabai, Surdas.
Worship of a formless and abstract God. Followers strongly opposed idol worship. Examples: Kabir, Guru Nanak.
South Indian Vaishnava saints who were devoted to Lord Vishnu. Their total number is traditionally considered to be 12.
South Indian Shaiva saints who were devoted to Lord Shiva. Their total number is traditionally considered to be 63.

important_facts.fact: The Bhakti movement originated in South India between the 7th and 9th centuries CE through the Alvar and Nayanar saints.
Ramananda was the first saint to bring the Bhakti movement from South India to North India.

sections.title: Prominent Bhakti Saints and their Philosophical Doctrines
sections.description: Key Vedanta philosophies proposed by various Bhakti saints explaining the relationship between God (Brahman) and the Soul (Atman).

key_associations.extra_info: Principle: 'Brahman is truth, the world is an illusion'. The individual soul and God are completely identical.
Principle: The soul is a part of God (Brahman), but it retains its individual identity even after liberation.
Principle: The individual soul (Jivatma) and the Supreme Soul (Paramatma) are entirely distinct entities.
Also known as the Bhedabheda philosophy; it states that the soul is both different and non-different from God.
He emphasized devotion to Lord Krishna and founded the 'Pushtimarg' (Path of Grace).

sections.title: Concepts of Sufi Movement
sections.description: Key terms and practices associated with the mystical and liberal dimensions of Islam.

key_concepts.explanation: A mystical sect of Islam that emphasizes attaining God (Allah) through deep personal love, devotion, and inner purity.
A Sufi hospice or rest house where Sufi saints lived, preached, and interacted with their disciples and the masses.
In the Sufi tradition, a spiritual teacher or guide is called a 'Pir', and the disciple or follower is called a 'Murid'.
'Ba-Shara' Sufis strictly followed the Islamic law (Sharia), whereas 'Be-Shara' Sufis (like wandering ascetics) did not bind themselves to the Sharia.

sections.title: Major Sufi Orders (Silsilas) in India
sections.description: Various Sufi orders that developed and gained popularity in the Indian subcontinent and their founders.

key_associations.extra_info: The most popular order in India; its main shrine (Dargah) is in Ajmer. They believed in musical gatherings (Qawwali) to connect with God.
Unlike the Chishtis, this order accepted state patronage, held government posts, and did not believe in a life of strict poverty.
The Mughal prince Dara Shikoh was a staunch follower and scholar of this particular Sufi order.
The most orthodox Sufi order that strictly opposed music (Sama); the Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb was one of its followers.

important_facts.fact: Sheikh Nizamuddin Auliya of the Chishti order was widely known by the title 'Mahbub-i-Ilahi' (Beloved of God).
The verses and teachings of the Sufi saint Baba Farid are respectfully included in the Sikh holy book, the Guru Granth Sahib.

sections.title: Important Literature and Compositions
sections.description: Major literary works composed by Bhakti and Sufi saints that significantly contributed to the development of regional languages.

key_associations.extra_info: A renowned compilation of Kabir's teachings, couplets (Dohas), and hymns.
An epic poem recounting the life of Lord Rama, composed in the Awadhi dialect. Tulsidas was a contemporary of Emperor Akbar.
Composed in the Braj language, it vividly describes the childhood miracles and divine play (Leela) of Lord Krishna.
An epic Sufi love poem (Premakhyan) composed in the Awadhi dialect.
He was a major proponent of Vaishnavism in Assam and is credited with creating the classical Sattriya Dance.
